question: Define a function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ by $f(n)=n+1$ when $n$ is odd and $f(n)=n-1$ when $n$ is even. Prove that $f$ is both one-one and onto.
explanation:
Verification of one-one property
Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and suppose $f(m)=f(n)$. If both $m$ and $n$ are odd, then $$m+1=n+1\Rightarrow m=n$$ If both are even, then $$m-1=n-1\Rightarrow m=n$$ Suppose $m$ is odd and $n$ is even. Equality of images would give $$m+1=n-1\Rightarrow n-m=2$$ But adding $2$ to an odd number gives an odd number, whereas $n$ is assumed even. This is impossible. Similarly, the case in which $m$ is even and $n$ is odd is impossible. Therefore, $f(m)=f(n)$ implies $m=n$, so $f$ is one-one.

Verification of onto property
Let $y\in\mathbb{N}$. If $y$ is odd, choose $$n=y+1$$ Then $n$ is even, and therefore $$f(n)=n-1=(y+1)-1=y$$ If $y$ is even, choose $$n=y-1$$ Then $n$ is odd and belongs to $\mathbb{N}$, and therefore $$f(n)=n+1=(y-1)+1=y$$ Thus, every natural number has a pre-image under $f$. Hence, $f$ is onto.

Final Result
The given function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is both one-one and onto.

options.A: $f$ is one-one but not onto because the natural number $1$ has no pre-image.
options.B: $f$ is both one-one and onto; each odd number $y$ has the pre-image $y+1$, and each even number $y$ has the pre-image $y-1$.
options.C: $f$ is onto but not one-one because every pair of consecutive natural numbers has the same image.
options.D: $f$ is neither one-one nor onto because the definition of $f$ depends on whether the input is odd or even.
